slides.title: AST 101 Week 3: Seasons
body_text: Why summer is warm
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Today's opening question is one most graduates get wrong when asked on camera.

slides.title: Quick Poll: What Causes the Seasons?
body_text: Distance from the Sun
Changes in the Sun's output
The tilt of Earth's axis
Something else
slides.speaker_notes: Distance is the favorite answer. Keep the tally for the end of class.

slides.title: Earth's Orbit Is Nearly Circular
body_text: Closest to the Sun (perihelion): about 147 million km, in early January
Farthest (aphelion): about 152 million km, in early July
A 3 percent difference cannot explain the seasons
slides.speaker_notes: And when it is summer in the north it is winter in the south. Same Earth, same distance.

slides.title: The Tilt
body_text: Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees
The axis keeps pointing toward Polaris all year
Each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for half of the orbit
slides.speaker_notes: Carry a tilted globe around a lamp. Do not let the axis wobble; it does not.

slides.title: Angle of Sunlight
body_text: Direct sunlight concentrates its energy on a small area
Slanted sunlight spreads the same energy over a larger area
Flashlight demonstration: count the squares on graph paper
slides.speaker_notes: Straight down: a small bright circle. Tilted: a large dim oval. Summer and winter.

slides.title: Day Length
body_text: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has longer days
At 47 degrees north: about 16 hours of daylight in June, about 8.5 in December
Longer days plus more direct light give summer
slides.speaker_notes: Two effects, one cause. Both come from the tilt.

slides.title: Solstices and Equinoxes
body_text: June solstice, about June 21: Sun farthest north
December solstice, about December 21: Sun farthest south
March and September equinoxes, about March 20 and September 22: Sun over the equator
At the equinoxes day and night are about equal everywhere
slides.speaker_notes: Solstice means the Sun stands still: its noon height stops climbing and turns back.

slides.title: Noon Sun Altitude
body_text: Altitude at noon = 90 degrees - latitude + the Sun's declination
The Sun's declination: +23.5 in June, 0 at the equinoxes, -23.5 in December
Example: at latitude 40 north in June, 90 - 40 + 23.5 = 73.5 degrees
slides.speaker_notes: Check with shadows: a low Sun casts long shadows.

slides.title: Where the Sun Rises
body_text: Equinoxes: due east, setting due west
June: north of east, setting north of west
December: south of east, setting south of west
slides.speaker_notes: Observing log: record where the Sun sets against a landmark, twice, two weeks apart.

slides.title: Seasonal Lag
body_text: Most sunlight arrives at the June solstice
The hottest weather comes weeks later
Oceans and land take time to warm up and cool down
slides.speaker_notes: Same reason the hottest time of day is mid-afternoon, not noon.
